opus.why: This is an editorial structure critique of an episode the audience will watch. A useful answer has to see that beats 4-6 set up the shame twist in beat 9, not just say whether they overlap. That takes real narrative judgment.

fable.why: "Review" here is editorial pacing judgment on a video outline, not code review. Needs to see that beats 4-6 all express 'no external pressure' and propose a merge or reorder with reasoning about flow. Sonnet at high handles structural story critique without a visible quality gap; it is analysis, not final audience copy.

opus.why: Turning a small Mermaid graph into a grouped checklist is mechanical. Each box and arrow becomes one item, so there's almost nothing to judge.

fable.why: "Translate" is a mechanical transform: 12 nodes and 13 arrows from a small mermaid file into a grouped checklist. No judgment, just complete coverage and grouping. Haiku at its default effort does this reliably on a diagram this size.

opus.why: This is tagline wording for a brand, the most visible copy there is. Getting away from the energy-drink feel and toward solar garden lights takes careful word choice.

fable.why: Tagline word choice is the highest-stakes brand copy the audience reads. Must avoid the energy-drink connotation, fit solar garden lights, and keep the line's rhythm, with a bilingual brief. Sonnet produces plausible options but opus's taste in the final word is where quality shows.

opus.why: Comparing two headlines for the same audience is a bounded judgment about clickbait risk and the promise each one makes. Sonnet at high effort handles that well.

fable.why: Continues the headline-testing thread. The deliverable is a comparative judgment on clickbait risk versus the first headline for the same renters audience, with likely variants. Sonnet at high reasons well about platform norms and promise clarity; it is assessment rather than a finished brand line.

opus.why: Diagnosing and fixing the prose rhythm of a published brand story needs a fine ear for sentence cadence. This is final copy.

fable.why: "Debug" means diagnosing prose rhythm in the brand story intro, which is final audience copy. The owner can't name the problem, so the model needs a sharp ear: the long final sentence breaking the short-beat pattern, the comma splice, the paired contrasts. Opus's close-reading precision matters here.

opus.why: The job is to reorganize existing lines into sections like persona, do's, don'ts and examples without rewriting them. That needs light grouping judgment and no new copy.

fable.why: "Refactor" is restructuring a brandbook section into persona, principles, do/don't, examples, with the wording preserved verbatim. Requires sensible categories and zero dropped or altered sentences. Sonnet at medium does this cleanly; haiku risks paraphrasing or losing a line.

opus.why: Hooks for a short video are the copy viewers see first and decide on. Quality and variety matter most here.

fable.why: "Compile" is really generating 10 short-form hooks, which are the exact words the audience hears first. Variety, punch, and avoiding cliché across 10 options is where cheaper models flatten out. Opus at high holds the creative ceiling.

opus.why: This is a short post rewritten into natural, human Russian. The tone has to land because customers read it as final copy.

fable.why: Register rewrite of a short Russian maintenance notice from corporate to plain human. Audience-facing but low-stakes and formulaic; sonnet's Russian is strong and the task is small, so medium effort holds quality. Haiku could sound stiff or lose nuance.

opus.why: Most of this is a mechanical color swap. It also needs some care to flag the PNG with baked-in pins, the gradient's light-blue end stop, and how orange contrasts with the new green. Sonnet handles that well.

fable.why: "Deploy" means editing the deck outline markdown and flagging slides needing manual work: pins baked into a PNG, the gradient whose end tint derives from the old blue, contrast of the white logo on the new green. Needs some visual reasoning beyond find-and-replace, which sonnet at high catches; opus adds nothing here.
